[[File:Phormium colensoi - lesser NZ flax - seed pods.jpg|thumb|Pods]]
'''''Phormium colensoi''''' (syn. ''Phormium cookianum'' – see below), also called '''mountain flax''', or {{lang|mi|wharariki}} in [[Māori language|Māori]], is a perennial plant that is endemic to New Zealand.<ref name="DoC" /> The greenish, yellow or orange flowers are followed by twisted seed pods.<ref name="DoC" /> It is less common than the other ''[[Phormium]]'' species, ''[[Phormium tenax|P. tenax]]'' or {{lang|mi|harakeke}}. Mountain flax is also known as {{lang|mi|whararipi}}, {{lang|mi|whatariki}}, {{lang|mi|mangaeka}}, {{lang|mi|kōrari tuauru}} (Williams 1971), {{lang|mi|wauraki}} (Bell 1890 sic.),<ref name="maoriplantuse" /> coastal flax, hill flax<ref name="maoriplantuse" /> and lesser New Zealand flax.<ref name="BSBI07" />

==Description== 
The leaves are under 2 metres in length while those of ''P. tenax'' range from 1 to 3 metres in length.<ref name="Wardle1979" /> The [[Scape (botany)|scape]] is much shorter than that of ''P. tenax'', rising up to 2 metres in height while that of ''P. tenax'' is around 5 metres in height.<ref name="Wardle1979" /> The colour of the inner tepals is green while the outer tepals are yellow to red.<ref name="Wardle1979" /> In contrast the tepals of ''P. tenax'' are a dull red, with the tips of the inner tepals being less strongly recurved.<ref name="Wardle1979" /> The capsules of ''P. colensoi'', unlike those of ''P. tenax'' are twisted and pendulous, and may be twice as long (up to 20 cm in length).<ref name="Wardle1979" /> The numerous seeds in each pod are glossy black, flat and elongated with a frilled margin <ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/phormium-cookianum-subsp-cookianum/|title=Phormium cookianum |publisher= New Zealand Plant Conservation network|access-date=8 February 2023|date=1 June 2013}}</ref>

''Phormium colensoi'' has two distinct geographic forms, one occurring in lowland parts of the [[North Island]], and the other in the southern and mountainous areas of the [[South Island]] as well as ranges in the North Island. The lowland form has green or yellow tepals and the mountain form has red tepals.<ref name="Wardle1979" /> In the [[Cook Strait]] area, both forms and intermediates can be found.<ref name="Wardle1979" />

==Taxonomy==
The species was originally mentioned without description by [[William Colenso]], the name being given as ''Phormium forsterianum''.<ref name="FNZ" /><ref name="Colenso1844" /> It was later known as ''P. colensoi'', a name that was listed without description in 1846 by [[Joseph Dalton Hooker]].<ref name="yEwJM" /> The name became better known from J. D. Hooker's 1864 publication in ''Handbook of the New Zealand Flora''.<ref name="FNZ" /> However, previously, in 1848, [[Auguste François Le Jolis]] had described the species under the name ''P. cookianum'',<ref name="FNZ" /><ref name="04oIE" /> and for many years this name was thought to have [[Priority (nomenclature)|priority]] over Hooker's name ''P. colensoi''. The latter is now regarded as the accepted name by some, based on a brief description of the species in a quotation from J.D. Hooker in an article by Auguste Le Jolis in the ''Revue Horticole'' of 1 January 1848.<ref name="WCSP_Pc" /><ref name="leJolis1848" /> Another specimen, believed to be identical to a plant found by [[Ronald Campbell Gunn|Ronald Gunn]] at the [[Whanganui River]]<ref name="Earp2014" /> in 1864, was described from a plant growing in a garden in [[Torquay, England]] in 1888 and given the name ''P. hookeri'' (later reduced to a subspecies under the name ''P. cookianum'' subsp. ''hookeri'').<ref name="FNZ" /> This name is also now regarded as a synonym of ''P. colensoi'' by some.<ref name="WCSP_Ph" /> ''Phormium cookianum'',<ref name="LeJolis1848x" /> however, is still the preferred name in Aotearoa New Zealand according to Ngā Tipu Aotearoa<ref name="O4d14" /> and The Flora of New Zealand,<ref name="8Xxxs" /> as studies of the complex morphological and genetic variation<ref name="McBreen2003" /><ref name="Scheele2010" /><ref name="Smissen2008">{{cite journal |last1=Smissen |first1=R. D. |last2=Heenan |first2=P. B. |last3=Houliston |first3=G. J. |title=Genetic and morphological evidence for localised interspecific gene flow in Phormium (Hemerocallidaceae) |journal=New Zealand Journal of Botany |date=September 2008 |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=287–297 |doi=10.1080/00288250809509767|bibcode=2008NZJB...46..287S |s2cid=205448164 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Smissen2010c">{{cite journal |last1=Smissen |first1=R. D. |last2=Heenan |first2=P. B. |title=A taxonomic appraisal of the Chatham Islands flax (Phormium tenax) using morphological and DNA fingerprint data |journal=Australian Systematic Botany |date=2010 |volume=23 |issue=5 |pages=371 |doi=10.1071/SB10023 |bibcode=2010AuSyB..23..371S }}</ref> as well as hybridization,<ref name="Smissen2007">{{cite journal |last1=Smissen |first1=R. D. |last2=Heenan |first2=P. B. |title=DNA fingerprinting supports hybridisation as a factor explaining complex natural variation in Phormium (Hemerocallidaceae) |journal=New Zealand Journal of Botany |date=June 2007 |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=419–432 |doi=10.1080/00288250709509723|bibcode=2007NZJB...45..419S |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Houliston2008" /> and hence taxonomy, of the genus are still underway.

==Uses==
{{See also|Māori traditional textiles}}
Wharariki is a taonga (sacred, treasure) species to Māori and numerous traditional cultivars have been used for various purposes. Refer to Ngā Tipu Whakaoranga [Māōri Plant Use Database] and the citations within<ref name="maoriplantuse" /> and Te Kohinga Harakeke o Aotearoa – National New Zealand Flax Collection.<ref name="6HFHv" />

*''Wharariki'' - a variety from [[Urewera]] has a superior fibre quality that may be  woven into a soft kete [traditional Māori  basket]. It has a slight yellow colouration when dried.<ref name="Harakeke" />
*''Whakaari'' - a variety with leaves suitable for weaving kete, but less suitable than other cultivars for [[piupiu]] [Māori waist-to-knees garment made of flax - has a wide waistband and is used in modern times for kapa haka performances].<ref name="piupiu" /> The leaves have strong blades and dry naturally to a deep green colour, or to a pale greenish-fawn after being boiled for a minute.

==Cultivars==
Numerous [[cultivar]]s of this species have been selected for cultivation (those marked {{smallcaps|agm}} have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]):<ref name="wbpYQ" /> 
*'Black Adder' <ref name="RHS" />
*'Cream Delight'{{smallcaps|agm}}<ref name="CreamDelight" />
*'Dark Delight' has deep-red leaves up to 1.2 metres in length<ref name="Turner1999" />
*'Duet', a dwarf cultivar up to 30 cm in height with cream and green variegated foliage<ref name="Turner1999" />
*'Flamingo'<ref name="RHS" />
*'Golden Wonder'<ref name="RHS" />
*'Maori Maiden' (also known as 'Rainbow Maiden'), an erect growing cultivar with leaves to 1 metre in length with bronze stripes<ref name="Turner1999" />
*'Sundowner', a cultivar with very long leaves which are up to 1.8 metres long. These have a purple centre and cream edges.<ref name="Turner1999" />
*'Tricolor',{{smallcaps|agm}}<ref name="Tricolor" /> an upright cultivar that has leaves with red, yellow and green stripes. The flowers are pale yellowish-green.<ref name="Turner1999" />

There is also a dwarf cultivar, and hybrid cultivars have been selected from crosses with ''Phormium tenax''.<ref name="RHS" /> ''P. colensoi'' cultivars are regarded as less hardy than other ''Phormium'' cultivars.<ref name="Fernwood" />

==See also==
*[[Exocarpic acid]], a rare fatty acid found in the plant.
